hook.text: A turbocharger turns exhaust waste into extra power—free energy from stuff you'd throw away.

buildup.text: Exhaust gases spin a turbine at up to 150,000 RPM. That turbine drives a compressor on a shared shaft.

discovery.text: The compressor forces extra air into the engine. More air means more fuel can burn, so more power.

twist.text: Turbo lag is the delay before the turbine spins fast enough. You press the gas and wait a beat.

climax.text: Modern twin-scroll and electric turbos nearly eliminate lag, giving instant response.

details.summary: A turbocharger uses exhaust gas energy to spin a turbine that compresses incoming air, forcing more oxygen into the engine cylinders to produce significantly more power from the same displacement.
details.whyItMatters: Turbocharging lets smaller engines match the power of larger ones while using less fuel at light loads, enabling the global trend of engine downsizing that improves fleet fuel economy.
takeaways: Exhaust gases spin a turbine connected to a compressor
Compressed air allows more fuel to burn per combustion cycle
Turbo lag is the delay before boost pressure builds up

faq.question: Does turbocharging reduce engine life?
faq.answer: Modern turbocharged engines are designed for the extra stress and are very reliable with proper maintenance. Using correct oil, allowing brief cool-down periods, and regular service keep them healthy.

faq.question: What is turbo lag and can it be eliminated?
faq.answer: Turbo lag is the delay between pressing the accelerator and feeling boost as the turbine spins up. Twin-scroll turbos, electric compressors, and variable geometry vanes have greatly reduced but not eliminated it.
